answers: In recent decades, many new regulations intended to strengthen financial soundness, improve consumer protections, and aid anti-money laundering efforts were implemented for financial institutions. Smaller community banks and credit unions must comply with some of the regulations, but compliance can be more challenging and costly for these institutions. GAO examined (1) the regulations community banks and credit unions viewed as most burdensome and why, and (2) efforts by depository institution regulators to reduce any regulatory burden. GAO analyzed regulations and interviewed more than 60 community banks and credit unions (selected based on asset size and financial activities), regulators, and industry associations and consumer groups. GAO also analyzed letters and transcripts commenting on regulatory burden that regulators prepared responding to the comments. Interviews and focus groups GAO conducted with representatives of over 60 community banks and credit unions indicated regulations for reporting mortgage characteristics, reviewing transactions for potentially illicit activity, and disclosing mortgage terms and costs to consumers were the most burdensome. Institution representatives said these regulations were time-consuming and costly to comply with, in part because the requirements were complex, required individual reports that had to be reviewed for accuracy, or mandated actions within specific timeframes. However, regulators and others noted that the regulations were essential to preventing lending discrimination and use of the banking system for illicit activity, and they were acting to reduce compliance burdens. Institution representatives also said that the new mortgage disclosure regulations increased compliance costs, added significant time to loan closings, and resulted in institutions absorbing costs when others, such as appraisers and inspectors, changed disclosed fees. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) issued guidance and conducted other outreach to educate institutions after issuing these regulations in 2013. But GAO found that some compliance burdens arose from misunderstanding the disclosure regulations—which in turn may have led institutions to take actions not actually required. Assessing the effectiveness of the guidance for the disclosure regulations could help mitigate the misunderstandings and thus also reduce compliance burdens. Regulators of community banks and credit unions—the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and the National Credit Union Administration—conduct decennial reviews to obtain industry comments on regulatory burden. But the reviews, conducted under the Economic Growth and Regulatory Paperwork Reduction Act of 1996 (EGRPRA), had the following limitations: CFPB and the consumer financial regulations for which it is responsible were not included. Unlike executive branch agencies, the depository institution regulators are not required to analyze and report quantitative-based rationales for their responses to comments. Regulators do not assess the cumulative burden of the regulations they administer. CFPB has formed an internal group that will be tasked with reviewing regulations it administers, but the agency has not publicly announced the scope of regulations included, the timing and frequency of the reviews, and the extent to which they will be coordinated with the other federal banking and credit union regulators as part of their periodic EGRPRA reviews. Congressional intent in mandating that these regulators review their regulations was that the cumulative effect of all federal financial regulations be considered. In addition, sound practices required of other federal agencies require them to analyze and report their assessments when reviewing regulations. Documenting in plans how the depository institution regulators would address these EGRPRA limitations would better ensure that all regulations relevant to community banks and credit unions were reviewed, likely improve the analyses the regulators perform, and potentially result in additional burden reduction. GAO makes a total of 10 recommendations to CFPB and the depository institution regulators. CFPB should assess the effectiveness of guidance on mortgage disclosure regulations and publicly issue its plans for the scope and timing of its regulation reviews and coordinate these with the other regulators' review process. As part of their burden reviews, the depository institution regulators should develop plans to report quantitative rationales for their actions and addressing the cumulative burden of regulations. In written comments, CFPB and the four depository institution regulators generally agreed with the recommendations.

This report by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) examines the regulatory compliance burdens on community banks and credit unions, and the efforts of federal regulators to mitigate these costs. While community banks and credit unions are generally defined as smaller institutions with local management, they face significant compliance costs that larger banks can better absorb due to a lack of economies of scale.

Interviews and focus groups with 64 institutions identified three primary regulatory areas as most burdensome: the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA), Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) requirements, and the Truth-in-Lending/Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act Integrated Disclosure (TRID) rule. Representatives cited the complexity, time consumption, and cost of these regulations, noting that HMDA and BSA/AML requirements often divert staff time from customer service. While consumer advocates and regulators argue these rules are essential for fair lending and national security, the institutions report that the costs are high and sometimes unnecessary.

To address these burdens, regulators have utilized the Economic Growth and Regulatory Paperwork Reduction Act (EGRPRA) process. In the 2017 review, regulators proposed changes to capital rules, Call Reports, and appraisal requirements to reduce paperwork. However, the GAO found limitations in the EGRPRA process. Specifically, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) was not included in the review, meaning key regulations it administers were not assessed. Additionally, regulators did not conduct or report on quantitative analyses to assess the cumulative impact of regulations, and they did not evaluate how different regulations might overlap or duplicate requirements.

The GAO made 10 recommendations to improve the regulatory review process. These include requiring CFPB to assess the effectiveness of its TRID guidance and to publicly outline its review plans, and directing the Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC, and NCUA to develop plans for conducting quantitative analyses and evaluating the cumulative effects of regulations. The agencies generally agreed with the findings and recommendations.

This report by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) examines the regulatory burdens facing community banks and credit unions. While these institutions are generally defined as smaller, locally focused entities, they face a complex web of federal requirements. The report highlights that the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act, intended to strengthen oversight, has created significant compliance costs for these smaller institutions, despite exemptions designed to protect them.

The GAO found that community banks and credit unions identified three specific regulations as the most burdensome: the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA), the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA/AML), and the Truth-in-Lending Act/Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (TRID). Institutions reported that HMDA and TRID requirements were complex and time-consuming, often requiring extensive staff training and data reporting. Additionally, BSA/AML requirements were viewed as costly and complex, with some institutions feeling that the regulations did not account for the scale of their operations.

To address these concerns, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) has taken steps to reduce the burden associated with these regulations. For example, the CFPB has issued guidance to help community banks and credit unions understand the requirements, and has implemented new online systems for submitting data. The GAO also noted that the CFPB has not assessed the effectiveness of its TRID guidance, and that some community banks and credit unions were confused about the regulations.

The report concludes that while regulators have made efforts to reduce the burden, there are still significant challenges. The GAO recommends that the CFPB assess the effectiveness of its TRID guidance and issue public information on its plans for reviewing regulations. The report also recommends that the federal depository institution regulators develop plans for conducting regulatory analyses to strengthen the rigor and transparency of their EGRPRA reviews. The GAO found that the regulators generally agreed with these recommendations.
